1240.title: Rose and Martin
1240.hook: a broom and a garden hut: the saints of Lima were both Dominican
1240.howItsDone: Catholics in Peru and far beyond honor Saint Rose of Lima and Saint Martin de Porres with feast days, processions and prayers; Dominican churches in Lima keep their shrines.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a sermon on Hispaniola. Your line was are these not men.

Two objects from one city. The first is a broom. It belongs to a Dominican brother in Lima, in Peru, who sweeps the cloister, the infirmary and the kitchen every day. The city nicknames him Brother Broom. The second is a tiny hut at the bottom of a family garden in the same city, barely big enough to kneel in. A young woman prays there among the flowers she grows and sells to help her family. The broom belonged to Martin de Porres, the hut to Rose of Lima. Today, two saints, one city, one white habit.
screen: `A BROOM IN A PRIORY.` → `A HUT IN A FAMILY GARDEN.` → `ONE CITY, ONE WHITE HABIT.`

segments.voice: You met each in year three; today, both together. Lima under Spanish rule was a city of Spaniards, Indigenous Peruvians, Africans enslaved and free, and people of mixed ancestry, sorted by strict lines of rank. Martin was born on the wrong side of those lines. His father was a Spanish nobleman; his mother, a free woman of African descent. When he asked to join the Dominicans, he was taken in as a helper, not a full brother. He swept. He cut hair. He nursed the sick in the priory and the streets, and gave away whatever came into his hands. Stories gathered around him, including his gentleness with animals, even the priory's mice. In time the brothers received him as a lay brother. Rose took a different road to the same family. Like Catherine of Siena, the mantellata, she stayed home as a Dominican laywoman, and tradition says she took Catherine as her model. Her needle and garden supported her parents, and part of the house became a place to care for the sick and poor. She also practiced hard penances that can be difficult to read about today, and her biographers don't hide them. Tradition says Rose and Martin knew each other. Each found Christ in the people their city looked past. Jesus says it plainly in Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me."

1241.title: The Inquisition, honestly
1241.hook: church courts that used coercion and handed people to execution; John Paul II asked forgiveness
1241.howItsDone: The Catholic Church has publicly confessed sins committed by its members in the use of force in the service of faith, notably in a Day of Pardon liturgy led by John Paul II; Catholics pray for the dead, including victims of religious violence, at Mass and with prayers such as 'Eternal rest'.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rose and Martin, a garden hut and a broom. Your line was lima's saints.

A Sunday in Lent, in Saint Peter's Basilica in Rome. Pope John Paul II stands before a crucifix. One after another, cardinals step forward and name sins committed by members of the Church, and after each one the pope asks God's forgiveness. One confession is for sins committed in the service of truth: intolerance, and force used against others in the name of faith. The cardinal who reads it leads the Vatican office that grew out of the old Roman Inquisition. Today, the hardest part of the Dominican story, honestly.
screen: `A SUNDAY IN LENT, SAINT PETER'S.` → `SINS IN THE SERVICE OF TRUTH.` → `THE HARDEST PART, HONESTLY.`

segments.voice: You met inquisitions in passing on day eight hundred forty-five. Inquisition comes from the Latin inquisitio, an inquiry, a legal investigation. It wasn't one court. In medieval Europe, popes appointed inquisitors to investigate heresy, among them friars, Dominicans and Franciscans. Later came the Spanish Inquisition, run under the Spanish crown, which pursued people whose families had converted from Judaism or Islam and who were suspected of keeping their old faith in secret. Then the Roman Inquisition. The courts questioned people. They used coercion, and at times torture. When someone was judged a heretic and wouldn't recant, the court handed them over to the civil authorities, who put them to death. The Church didn't light the fire, but it handed the person to the ones who did. Historians argue about the numbers, and popular stories sometimes inflate them. That doesn't change the core: the same order that preached veritas sometimes served this. So what does the Gospel say about force? When a Samaritan village refuses to welcome Jesus, James and John offer to call down fire from heaven. Luke says Jesus turns and rebukes them, and they go on to another village. And on the night he's arrested, when a disciple draws a sword, Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Put up again thy sword into its place." So the confession in Saint Peter's matters. The Church said, in public, that people who believed they were serving the truth did it with force, and that this was sin. It wasn't explained away. Forgiveness was asked.
screen: `INQUISITIO: AN INQUIRY, A COURT.` · `MEDIEVAL, SPANISH, ROMAN.` · `COERCION, AND HANDING PEOPLE OVER TO DIE.` · `JESUS REBUKES THE CALL FOR FIRE.` · then, large: `PUT UP AGAIN THY SWORD INTO ITS PLACE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people who stood before those courts, whose names we will never know, Jews and Muslims and their descendants, people judged heretics, and then everyone, of any faith or none, hurt or killed by someone acting in the name of God. Just hold them in silence. If you pray, you can say, "Eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord," the Church's old prayer for the dead, and if not, let the quiet be your respect.
Inquisition. Church courts that investigated heresy, used coercion, and handed people over to be executed; a history the Church has publicly asked forgiveness for. Today's word.
Your line: forgiveness asked. Named out loud, before a crucifix, and not explained away. Rest well.

1242.title: Lacordaire (1850)
1242.hook: a famous preacher restores the Dominicans in France
1242.howItsDone: French Dominicans remember Lacordaire as the friar who restored their order in France, and some Catholic preachers still point to his Notre-Dame sermons as an example of speaking to people who doubt.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Inquisition, told honestly, and a pope who later asked forgiveness for wrongs done in the Church's name. Your line was forgiveness asked.

Paris. A cathedral full to the doors, and in the pulpit a young priest whose sermons don't sound like the ones people grew up with. He talks about freedom, about doubt, about the questions students argue over late at night. People who hadn't set foot in a church in a long time come to Notre-Dame to hear him. Then, at the height of it, he leaves for Rome. When he comes back, he is dressed in white: the habit of the Dominicans, an order the upheavals of the Revolution had pushed out of France. His name was Henri Lacordaire.
screen: `A FULL CATHEDRAL IN PARIS.` → `HE LEAVES FOR ROME.` → `HE COMES BACK IN WHITE.`

segments.voice: Lacordaire took the religious name Dominique, after the founder, and set out to do something that sounded impossible: gather men to live as Dominican friars in France again. The way he did it is the lesson. Yesterday's courts tried to force belief. Lacordaire went the other way. Before he was a friar, he had helped run a newspaper arguing that the Church should ask nothing from governments except freedom: to teach, to gather, to preach. When the pope rejected some of the paper's ideas, Lacordaire accepted the ruling and stayed. He didn't win by shouting, and he didn't leave by slamming the door. When he asked for the friars to return, he appealed to the same liberty every citizen claimed, not to a special favor. And when he preached, the story goes, he spoke to doubters as people worth talking to, not as enemies to defeat. The first letter of Peter puts it in two steps. In the Douay-Rheims, believers are told to be "ready always to satisfy every one that asketh you a reason of that hope which is in you." Then the next verse begins: "But with modesty and fear." A reason, and modesty. Lacordaire held both. For him, preaching wasn't volume. It was respect with a reason inside it.

1243.title: Lay Dominicans
1243.hook: laypeople who pray, study and share
1243.howItsDone: Lay Dominicans gather in local fraternities, meeting to pray part of the Liturgy of the Hours, study together and plan works of service; after a time of formation, members make a promise to live by the order's rule for the laity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lacordaire, the preacher who came home in a white habit and brought the friars back to France. Your line was back to france.

A Tuesday evening in a parish hall. Folding chairs, a coffee urn, a plate of store-bought cookies. Around the table: a nurse still in scrubs, a retired mechanic, a college student, a grandmother with a well-thumbed Bible full of sticky notes. They open with a psalm, prayed back and forth across the table. Then someone reads a short passage, and they argue about it, politely, for an hour. Nobody here wears a habit. Everyone goes home to a mortgage or a roommate or a sink full of dishes. And every one of them, by promise, belongs to the Order of Preachers.
screen: `A PARISH HALL ON A TUESDAY.` → `A PSALM, A PASSAGE, AN ARGUMENT.` → `NO HABITS. ALL DOMINICANS.`

segments.voice: Lay Dominicans are laypeople, married or single, with ordinary jobs, who make a promise to live the Dominican way inside an ordinary life. The Dominicans speak of themselves as a family with several branches: friars, cloistered nuns, sisters in active work, and laypeople. Same motto, same founder, different kitchens. What do the laypeople do? The same three things this stretch keeps circling. Pray: a lay Dominican may take up part of the Church's daily prayer, the psalms of morning or evening. Study: not for a degree, but because Dominicans hold that you can't share what you haven't chewed on. And share, which is the surprising part, because the order's name is preachers. A layperson doesn't preach from a pulpit at Mass. So where? At work, at home, over a fence, in how they answer a hard question from a teenager. Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven." A light doesn't give a speech. It shines where it is. That's the lay preacher's pulpit: wherever they already stand. And they don't do it alone. The fraternity, the small local group, meets to pray and study together, because a question argued over with friends gets sharper than one carried alone.
screen: `A PROMISE, LIVED IN AN ORDINARY LIFE.` · `ONE FAMILY: FRIARS, NUNS, SISTERS, LAITY.` · `PRAY, STUDY, SHARE.` · `THE PULPIT IS WHERE YOU STAND.` · then, large: `SO LET YOUR LIGHT SHINE BEFORE MEN.`

Lay Dominicans. Laypeople who promise to live the Dominican way at home and at work: praying, studying together, and sharing what they learn. Today's word.

1244.title: Frassati the Dominican
1244.hook: Pier Giorgio was a lay Dominican
1244.howItsDone: Some young Catholics in parish and campus groups take Pier Giorgio Frassati as a patron, and some organize hikes and climbs under his motto, verso l'alto.

segments.voice: Yesterday, lay Dominicans: people with jobs and families who promise to pray, study and share where they stand. Your line was lay preachers.

An old black-and-white photograph. A young man in a hat and climbing gear, roped, leaning into a steep slope of rock. Across the bottom, in his own handwriting, a short Italian phrase: verso l'alto. Toward the top. He was a student in Turin from a well-known family, who could have spent his life comfortably. Friends remembered him as loud, funny, a practical joker, quick to suggest a hike. And quietly, he had joined yesterday's people. Pier Giorgio Frassati was a lay Dominican.
screen: `A PHOTO ON A ROCK FACE.` → `HIS OWN WORDS: VERSO L'ALTO.` → `A LAY DOMINICAN IN CLIMBING GEAR.`

segments.voice: You met Pier Giorgio back on day nine hundred sixteen, at his funeral; today, his Dominican side. When he made his promise as a lay Dominican, he took a new name in the order: Girolamo, Jerome. He kept his ordinary life. He studied engineering, argued politics, went to Mass, and dragged his friends up mountains. But the Dominican three, pray, study, share, ran underneath all of it. The sharing is the part his own family didn't see. By his friends' accounts, he visited the poor of Turin, bringing food, paying for medicine, giving away what he had, sometimes even his fare home, so that he walked. He didn't announce it. When he died young, after a sudden illness, the story told about his funeral is that the streets filled with poor people his parents had never met. That is a lay preacher's sermon: preached without a pulpit, and heard only at the end. And the mountains weren't a break from faith. They were part of it. The Psalms in the Douay-Rheims say: "I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from whence help shall come to me." Climbing was a way of going toward God with your whole body, roped to a friend, step by step. Verso l'alto. The Church holds him up as a model for young people, and his phrase has become a kind of motto: not a call to be grim or perfect, but to keep climbing, with friends, toward the summit.

1245.title: Yves Congar
1245.hook: a Dominican once silenced, later an architect of Vatican II
1245.howItsDone: Catholic theologians and students still read Congar on the Church, the laity and Christian unity, and his name comes up often when Catholics talk about how Vatican II's teaching took shape.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Frassati the Dominican: a climber in Turin who wrote toward the top on a photo and gave away his fare home. Your line was verso l'alto.

A French friar packs a suitcase. He is a scholar of the Church, a man who lives among books and footnotes, and he has just been told by his superiors, under pressure from Rome, that he may no longer teach. What he writes now must be checked before anyone reads it. He is sent away from Paris, from his students, from his work. He doesn't storm off. He doesn't leave the order. He goes. Years later, the same man would sit in the hall of a council of the whole Church, helping bishops write the documents they would vote on. Same friar. Same ideas.
screen: `A SCHOLAR PACKS A SUITCASE.` → `NO MORE TEACHING.` → `LATER: A SEAT AT THE COUNCIL.`

segments.voice: Yves Congar was a Dominican theologian who spent his life on one large question: what is the Church, and how does it renew itself without losing itself? He wrote about reform, about the role of laypeople, about Christians of other churches as brothers and sisters to be listened to. One of his books is called True and False Reform in the Church. In his time some of these ideas looked dangerous to authorities in Rome, and he was restricted: no teaching, no publishing without permission, sent from place to place. His journals, published after his death, show how much it hurt. And yet he obeyed. Not because he thought he was wrong, but because, for him, staying inside the Church was part of what reform meant. True reform, he argued, is patient. It doesn't break the body to heal it. Then the wind changed. Pope John the Twenty-Third called the Second Vatican Council, and Congar was brought in as an expert. Ideas he had been silenced for helped shape what the council wrote about the Church and about other Christians. Near the end of his life, Pope John Paul II made him a cardinal. The letter of James, in the Douay-Rheims, has a farmer for this: "Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth: patiently bearing till he receive the early and latter rain." You plant, and you wait for weather you don't control. Patience is not the same as giving up.

1246.title: Fra Angelico's cells
1246.hook: each friar's cell at San Marco has its own fresco to pray with
1246.howItsDone: Some Catholics keep an icon, a crucifix or a holy picture in the place they pray at home, and San Marco in Florence, now a museum, still shows Fra Angelico's frescoes in the friars' cells.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yves Congar: silenced, obedient, and later called in to help shape a council. Your line was vindicated later.

A stone staircase in an old friary in Florence. You climb it, turn at the top, and on the wall in front of you is an angel, wings striped like a bird's, bowing to a young woman on a bench. Mary leans forward, arms crossed over her chest, listening. The colors are soft, the room plain, almost empty. Then you walk down the corridor, and every small doorway opens on a bare room with a single window and one more painting on the wall. A different one in each. This is San Marco, and the painter was a friar who lived there.
screen: `A STAIRCASE IN FLORENCE.` → `AN ANGEL BOWS TO MARY.` → `ONE PAINTING IN EVERY ROOM.`

segments.voice: You met the painter back on day eight hundred thirty-four; today, why his rooms look the way they do. He was a Dominican, Fra Giovanni, remembered as Fra Angelico, the angelic brother. With his workshop he painted frescoes on the walls of the friars' cells, the small rooms where each brother slept, studied and prayed. These were not made for visitors. They were made for one man at a time, to pray with, alone. So they are quiet on purpose: few details, plain backgrounds, nothing to distract. And in several of them there's a surprise. Off to the side of the Gospel scene stands a Dominican friar, sometimes Saint Dominic himself, simply watching. The friar in his cell looks at the wall and sees a friar inside the story: this is where you belong, at the edge of the scene, paying attention. At the top of the stairs, the Annunciation sets the tone for the house. Luke's Gospel gives Mary's answer, in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word." Listening, then yes. That's the Dominican rhythm this week has followed in different clothes: Rose and Martin in Lima, an honest look at the Inquisition, Lacordaire back in France, laypeople with a study group, a climber in Turin, a theologian who waited. And here, a painter who gave each brother a window into the Gospel, right next to his real window.

Picture what could go there, a small icon, a print, a photo, and for now just look at the spot and breathe, the way a friar might sit with his wall. If you pray, let Mary's answer, be it done to me, rest there.
Fra Angelico's cells. The rooms at San Marco in Florence, each with its own quiet fresco, painted by a Dominican friar for his brothers to pray with. Today's word.
Your line: a painting in each cell. Pray, study, share, and sometimes the sharing is a wall. See you tomorrow.
